description: We are a team of six software engineering students eager to share our creativity and ideas with the world while tackling a real-world problem and building something that can make a meaningful, positive impact!
summary: Field Shift is a crop-rotation planner that plans each field for the climate it will have, not the one it had. For every future rotation cycle, it projects the farm's agroclimate from 40 years of NASA POWER observations and, beyond ten years, from NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections under three SSP scenarios. It then searches for climate twins: places whose climate today matches the farm's future one. From 30 m national crop maps, it reads the crops and crop-to-crop transitions that farmers there actually grow on similar soil, and assembles the three best rotations for each section of the farm. Each rotation is scored on four priorities ranked by the farmer: yield, water, soil protection and pests. Field Shift also says whether to keep or change the current rotation. Unlike rotation tools calibrated on today's climate, Field Shift draws its evidence from the places where the farm's future climate is already being farmed. On six real farm sites in Canada and the United States, the twins move 173–311 km south as fields warm by 1.4–1.8 °C to 2056, and the adopted rotations stay within 2.9 points of their score for 30 years.
details:
Field Shift is a full-stack planning tool that combines climate projections, climate-analogue search, satellite vegetation data and agronomic rules to recommend crop rotations that will hold up as the climate changes. The farmer places the farm on a satellite map and draws its sections. For each section, they enter what grows there, the current rotation, past crops, known diseases and the seeds already on hand. They then choose the cycle length and horizon, and rank four priorities.

For each section and each cycle, the system works in six steps:

  1. It projects agroclimatic indicators: growing degree-days, summer rain, frost-free season and hot days.
  2. It searches about 350 NASA POWER grid cells for climate twins, using the sigma dissimilarity of Mahony et al.
  3. It keeps the twin fields with similar soil, using SoilGrids.
    • Yield: pre-crop effects measured from MODIS vigor and corrected for weather.
    • Water: a daily FAO-56 soil-water balance, with SMAP and ECOSTRESS for water stress.
    • Soil protection: living cover over time, plus RUSLE erosion and infiltration.
    • Pests: pressure from 43 soilborne organisms.

The results appear in a web interface:

  • a 3D farm planted with each year's crop;
  • the three proposed rotations side by side as crop wheels, next to the current one;
  • a "Climate & twins" map showing where the farm's future climate lives today.

Rota, the in-app assistant, explains every number in plain language.

The benefits are evidence and trust. Recommendations rest on rotations that farmers already practise under the target climate, not on rules tuned to a climate that is disappearing. Every input is open data read live and cached. When a service is down, the app says so instead of faking a value. Every number links to its source on a "Details & sources" page.

The intended impact is to help grain farmers adapt before the climate shifts, with healthier soils, fewer erosion and water losses, and diversified rotations. We tested the method on six contrasting sites: Saint-Hyacinthe (QC), Elora (ON), Carman (MB), Lethbridge (AB), Ames (IA) and Fargo (ND). At five of six sites, twins grow crops closer to the farm's own than cells chosen at the same distance without climate criteria. Our research paper also reports what must improve: an income objective, because the current scoring over-selects fallow, and 30 m NASA HLS imagery for sharper pre-crop effects.

We built the project with:

  • Python 3.11 (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, httpx) for the algorithm server: about 50 modules, parallel processing and an on-disk cache;
  • JavaScript (Vite, three.js, Leaflet) for the interface;
  • pytest and Vitest for testing;

The server reproduces our reference implementation on 17 field plans across 9 scenarios to 10⁻⁹.

The project is creative because, to our knowledge, it is the first use of climate analogues to constrain a field-scale rotation planner. It is a space-for-time approach in which other farm's present becomes evidence for your farm's future. It is also designed around how farmers decide: their own priorities, a simple keep-or-change answer, and rotations they can read at a glance.

We considered farmer control, cost (free, open data only), transparency and limits. A climate twin matches average climate, not day length, markets or local practice, and crop rules still need an agronomist's review. Field Shift supports the farmer's judgment; it does not replace it.
